opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason comes down to data and to how much of the relevant skill is already encoded in text. Social interaction, at least the part that matters economically, is overwhelmingly mediated through language. Negotiating, persuading, managing people, customer service, even a lot of emotional support: these happen in words, and we have an enormous corpus of humans doing exactly those things. Language models trained on that corpus pick up a lot of the implicit structure of how people respond to each other, what's polite, what's manipulative, what reassures someone. And we already see this. Models are surprisingly good at writing persuasively or reading the subtext of a message, often better than a typical person.

Sensorimotor tasks are different. There's this old observation, Moravec's paradox, that the things we find effortless, like walking across a cluttered room or picking up an egg without crushing it, turn out to be the hardest to automate. That's because evolution spent hundreds of millions of years optimizing those capabilities, so the underlying computation is enormous even though it feels trivial to us. Abstract reasoning and language are evolutionarily very recent, so in some sense there's less "hidden" complexity there.

On top of that, there's no internet-scale dataset of sensorimotor experience the way there is for text. You don't have trillions of tokens of fine-grained force feedback and proprioception from people folding laundry or fixing a sink. Collecting that data means physical robots operating in the real world, which is slow, expensive, and hard to parallelize. You can't just scrape it.

There's also the hardware bottleneck. Even if you solved the software side, you'd need cheap, reliable robot bodies with good actuators and sensors, and manufacturing those at scale takes time. Social interaction mostly just needs a screen, a microphone, or a text box, infrastructure that's already everywhere.

So my expectation is that AI gets very good at the social, language-heavy parts of jobs before it gets good at the physical parts. That has some counterintuitive implications: a lot of white-collar work involving communication may be automated before, say, plumbing or construction, which runs against the older intuition that "people skills" would be the last thing machines could do.

r001.rationale: The response says language and abstract reasoning are evolutionarily recent, but it does not attribute social interaction itself being easier to its being evolutionarily recent. It instead emphasizes language data and text-mediated social skills.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the basic reason comes down to how much data we have and how cheap it is to get more of it. Social interaction, at least the kind that happens through language, is extremely well represented in the training data we already have. Billions of people have written down how they argue, persuade, negotiate, console each other, flirt, joke. All of that is text, and text is cheap to collect and cheap to train on. So the model gets to see an enormous number of examples of humans interacting socially, and it can learn the structure of that pretty directly.

Sensorimotor tasks are different. If you want a robot to fold laundry or pick up an object it has never seen, there isn't a trillion-token corpus of robot arm trajectories lying around. You have to generate that data yourself, either by running physical robots, which is slow and expensive, or by simulation, which has the problem that the simulator never quite matches reality. So the data bottleneck is much more severe.

There's also the point that people often get backwards, which is that we tend to think of social skills as the sophisticated, uniquely human thing and motor control as the easy, animal thing. But evolution spent hundreds of millions of years optimizing motor control and perception, and only a few million years on language and complex social cognition. The stuff that feels effortless to us, like catching a ball or walking across a cluttered room, is actually where an enormous amount of hidden computation is happening. The stuff that feels hard, like reasoning through an argument or reading a room, is evolutionarily recent and comparatively shallow. That's basically Moravec's observation, and I think the last several years of AI progress have been a pretty strong confirmation of it.

The other thing I'd add is that social interaction through a chat interface has a very forgiving feedback loop. If the model says something slightly off, the human corrects it, or just moves on. Errors are cheap and recoverable. In the physical world, a small error compounds, you knock the glass over, and now the state of the world has changed in a way that's hard to undo. So the tolerance for imprecision is much lower, and you need the system to be reliable in a way that current models just aren't.

So when I say social interaction will be easier, I don't mean it's trivially solved. I mean that the ingredients that have driven progress so far, large amounts of data, cheap iteration, forgiving environments, all line up in favor of the social and linguistic side, and all line up against the sensorimotor side. I expect that gap to persist for a while, probably longer than a lot of people in the field assume.

r001.rationale: The response says language and complex social cognition evolved only a few million years ago, compared with hundreds of millions of years of evolution for motor control, and presents this as a reason social interaction is easier for AI.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of our intuition here comes from how difficult these things feel to us. Social interaction can require conscious thought, whereas picking up a cup feels effortless. But that doesn’t necessarily tell you how difficult those tasks are computationally. We have a lot of machinery for perception and motor control that operates without our being aware of it.

And for AI, there’s an enormous amount of training data about social interaction in text. You can learn quite a lot about what people believe, what they want, and how they’re likely to respond by learning to predict conversations. With physical tasks, you need to connect perception to action, and your actions change the environment you’re trying to learn about. Getting useful experience is also much more expensive if you need a robot to actually do things.

So I wouldn’t say every aspect of social interaction is easier than every sensorimotor task. But I don’t think we should be surprised if an AI can hold a sophisticated conversation or understand someone’s intentions before it can reliably do ordinary household chores.

r001.rationale: The response explains the expected difference through abundant text training data and the costs and complexity of physical interaction. It does not attribute social interaction’s relative ease to being evolutionarily more recent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that we have an enormous amount of data about human social interaction in the form of text. People describe what they want, explain why they did things, argue with each other, tell stories. So a language model gets a lot of information about how people think and how they respond to different situations just from learning to predict text.

With sensorimotor tasks, the connection between knowing what to do and actually doing it is much less direct. You can read a description of how to pick up a glass, but that doesn't give you the ability to control a hand, respond to the glass slipping, or judge how much force to apply. You need experience interacting with the physical world, and that experience is comparatively expensive to collect.

That doesn't mean every aspect of social interaction is easy. But I would expect AI to become quite good at understanding what someone means and figuring out an appropriate response before it becomes equally good at navigating an unfamiliar physical environment.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains the expectation through abundant text about social interaction and the need for physical-world experience for sensorimotor tasks. It does not attribute the difference to social interaction being evolutionarily more recent.
